plain_english: Everyone's problems come from external things. Everyone feels helpless about external things. "What should I do? How will this go? How will it end? Will this happen? Will that?" These are the words of people who focus on things outside their control. But who says "How can I avoid believing lies? How can I avoid turning away from truth?" If someone has such good sense to worry about these things, I'll remind him: Why worry? This is in your power. Be confident. Don't rush to agree with something before you test it against reason.
original_excerpt: The difficulties of all men are about external things, their helplessness is about external. What shall I do? how will it be? how will it turn out? will this happen? will that? All these are the words of those who are turning themselves to things which are not within the power of the will. For who says, How shall I not assent to that which is false? how shall I not turn away from the truth? If a man be of such a good disposition as to be anxious about these things I will remind him of this: Why are you anxious? The thing is in your own power, be assured; do not be precipitate in assenting before you apply the natural rule.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value

plain_english: Now suppose someone worries about their desires — they're afraid they won't get what they want. And they worry about avoiding things — they're afraid they'll run into exactly what they're trying to escape. First, I'd praise this person. Why? Because they've stopped caring about the stuff that makes everyone else anxious and fearful. They're focused on their own business and their own situation. Then I'd tell them: If you don't want to fail at getting what you desire, and you don't want to run into what you're avoiding, then follow this rule. Don't desire anything that belongs to other people. Don't try to avoid anything that's outside your control. If you ignore this rule, you're guaranteed to fail at your desires and hit exactly what you're trying to avoid. What's so hard about this? Where's the room for wondering 'How will this turn out?' or 'Will this happen or that?'
original_excerpt: On the other side, if a man is anxious (uneasy) about desire, lest it fail in its purpose and miss its end, and with respect to the avoidance of things, lest he should fall into that which he would avoid, I will first kiss (love) him, because he throws away the things about which others are in a flutter (others desire) and their fears, and employs his thoughts about his own affairs and his own condition. Then I shall say to him: If you do not choose to desire that which you will fail to obtain nor to attempt to avoid that into which you will fall, desire nothing which belongs to (which is in the power of) others, nor try to avoid any of the things which are not in your power. If you do not observe this rule, you must of necessity fail in your desires and fall into that which you would avoid. What is the difficulty here? where is there room for the words How will it be? and How will it turn out? and Will this happen or that?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value

plain_english: What's going to happen doesn't depend on your will, right? Yes. And whether something is good or evil — that depends on how your will responds to it, right? Yes. So can you handle whatever happens in the right way? Can anyone stop you from doing that? No one can. Then stop asking me "How will things turn out?" However they turn out, you'll handle them well. The outcome will be good for you. What would Hercules have been if he'd said "What if I don't face a great lion, or a great boar, or savage men?" Why do you even care about that?
original_excerpt: Now is not that which will happen independent of the will? Yes. And the nature of good and of evil, is it not in the things which are within the power of the will? Yes. Is it in your power then to treat according to nature everything which happens? Can any person hinder you? No man. No longer then say to me, How will it be? For, however it may be, you will dispose of it well, and the result to you will be a fortunate one. What would Hercules have been if he said: How shall a great lion not appear to me, or a great boar, or savage men? And what do you care for that?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value

plain_english: If a dangerous wild boar shows up, you'll fight an even bigger fight. If evil people show up, you'll rid the world of them. But suppose I die doing this? Then you'll die as a good person, doing something noble. Since everyone must die eventually, death will find each person doing something — farming, digging, trading, holding office, or suffering from stomach problems. So what do you want to be doing when death finds you? I would want to be found doing something truly human — something helpful, beneficial to everyone, and noble.
original_excerpt: If a great boar appear, you will fight a greater fight; if bad men appear, you will relieve the earth of the bad. Suppose then that I lose my life in this way. You will die a good man, doing a noble act. For since he must certainly die, of necessity a man must be found doing something, either following the employment of a husbandman, or digging, or trading, or serving in a consulship, or suffering from indigestion or from diarrhoea. What then do you wish to be doing when you are found by death? I, for my part, would wish to be found doing something which belongs to a man, beneficent, suitable to the general interest, noble.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value

plain_english: But if I can't achieve great things, at least I can do what nobody can stop me from doing — what I'm allowed to do. I can work on myself. I can develop my ability to handle impressions correctly. I can work toward freedom from destructive emotions. I can work toward peace of mind. I can fulfill my duties to others. If I succeed at these things, I can even advance to the third area: making sound judgments about things. If death catches me while I'm busy with this work, that's enough for me. I can stretch out my hands to God and say: 'The tools you gave me for understanding how you run the world and following your plan — I didn't neglect them. I didn't dishonor you with my actions. Look how I used my perceptions. Look how I used my basic concepts. Have I ever blamed you?'
original_excerpt: But if I cannot be found doing things so great, I would be found doing at least that which I cannot be hindered from doing, that which is permitted me to do, correcting myself, cultivating the faculty which makes use of appearances, laboring at freedom from the affects (laboring at tranquillity of mind); rendering to the relations of life their due. If I succeed so far, also (I would be found) touching on (advancing to) the third topic (or head) safety in forming judgments about things. If death surprises me when I am busy about these things, it is enough for me if I can stretch out my hands to God and say: The means which I have received from thee for seeing thy administration (of the world) and following it I have not neglected; I have not dishonored thee by my acts; see how I have used my perceptions, see how I have used my preconceptions; have I ever blamed thee?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value

plain_english: Have I been unhappy with anything that happens? Have I wished things were different? Have I tried to fight against the natural order of things? You gave me life, and I thank you for what you gave me. As long as I've used the things that belong to you, I'm content. Take them back and put them wherever you want — everything was yours to begin with. You just let me borrow them. Isn't it enough to leave this world with this attitude? What life is better than one lived with this mindset? What ending could be happier?
original_excerpt: have I been discontented with anything that happens, or wished it to be otherwise? have I wished to transgress the (established) relations (of things)? That thou hast given me life, I thank thee for what thou hast given. So long as I have used the things which are thine I am content. Take them back and place them wherever thou mayest choose, for thine were all things, thou gavest them to me. Is it not enough to depart in this state of mind? and what life is better and more becoming than that of a man who is in this state of mind? and what end is more happy?
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Ought to Despise and What Things We Ought to Value
